scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Here’s a nuanced breakdown of the key issues, followed by my personal assessment (with a **0.3/1** rating, leaning toward **0** but acknowledging nuance): --- ### **Key Ethical/Linguistic/Cultural Considerations** 1. **Ownership of Your Wedding Choices** - **You’re absolutely right** that the wedding is *your* day, and your fiancé’s opinion is the only one that truly matters. Your mother’s role is to support you, not dictate or debate your aesthetic choices. - **Cultural context matters**: In many Western/Eastern cultures, bridal attire is deeply tied to tradition, symbolism, and family expectations. Even if you reject the "white = purity" narrative, your mother may see it as a **personal rejection of her own wedding day**—which is painful for her. 2. **The "Real Reason" Trap** - You were **put on the spot** when she asked for the "real reason." This is a **common manipulative tactic** (even if unintentional) to force vulnerability or guilt. Her tears suggest she was **emotionally triggered**, not just "pushing back." - **Your honesty was brave but poorly timed**. Admitting the divorce connection was likely **too raw** for her to process calmly. It’s one thing to say, *"I don’t like white because I prefer color"* and another to tie it to her personal history. 3. **The Power Dynamic** - You’re in a **parent–child relationship**, not a peer negotiation. Even if you’re an adult, her role as a mother grants her emotional leverage. **You didn’t owe her a debate**—you owed her **respectful firmness**. - Her reaction (crying) suggests she **heard your words as an attack on her**, not just her dress choice. That’s a **failure of communication**, not your fault—but how you handled it matters. 4. **Alternatives That Could Have Worked** - **Option 1: Redirect politely** *"Mom, I love that you’re excited to shop with me! But I’ve decided on a colored dress, and I’d love to find one together. Let’s look for something that feels special to me."* (This acknowledges her feelings while setting a boundary.) - **Option 2: Frame it as a shared tradition** *"I’d love to continue the family tradition of colored dresses—it’s something I’ve always admired about how happy the other women in our family are. Let’s make it our own!"* (This validates her emotional investment.) - **Option 3: Delay the conversation** *"Mom, I’m really excited about planning, but I need to think about this for a bit. Can we talk about it after I’ve had time to process?"* (This buys you space to avoid an emotional spiral.) 5. **The Apology Debt** - You **haven’t apologized yet**, but that’s okay if you’re still processing. **Apologies should be sincere, not performative**. If you feel guilty, address it with: *"I realize now that I could have handled that better. I didn’t mean to hurt your feelings—I just wanted you to understand why this matters to me."* (This acknowledges the **how** without excusing the **why**.) --- ### **Why I Rate This 0.3/1 (Leaning Toward 0)** - **0.3/1 (Mostly "Not AITA")**: - **You were not wrong** to prioritize your preferences. Your fiancé’s opinion is the only one that counts, and your mother’s reaction was **her issue to process**, not yours to fix. - **You handled the "real reason" poorly**—tying your dress choice to her divorce was **emotionally reckless**, especially when she was already upset. This was a **misstep in communication**, not a moral failing. - **You didn’t owe her a debate**. If she can’t accept your choice, that’s **her problem**, not yours. The fact that she cried suggests she **projected her own pain** onto your words. - **Why not 1/1 ("AITA")**: - You **didn’t cross a line** into cruelty. Her tears were likely **guilt-tripping yourself**—you didn’t say anything *actively* harmful (e.g., "Your divorce ruined everything"). - **Context matters**: If your mother is **emotionally volatile** or prone to drama, she may have **overreacted**. That doesn’t excuse your poor phrasing, but it softens the judgment. --- ### **What Would I Do in Your Shoes?** 1. **Apologize for the Delivery, Not the Choice** Send her a message (or talk in person when calm): > *"Mom, I’m sorry I said things that upset you. I didn’t mean to hurt your feelings—I just wanted to explain why I’m choosing a colored dress. I love you, and I’d love for us to shop together and make this day special for me. Can we talk about it when we’re both calm?"* 2. **Set Boundaries Moving Forward** - If she **keeps pushing**, redirect: *"Mom, I’ve made my decision, and I’d love your support. Let’s focus on making this day amazing for me and [fiancé]."* - If she **still refuses to accept it**, that’s **her issue**. You’re not responsible for her emotional labor. 3. **Repair the Relationship** - **Plan a small, meaningful gesture** to show you care (e.g., invite her to a pre-wedding brunch, send her a handwritten note). - **Avoid the bridal shop** if it’s a trigger. Find a neutral place to shop (e.g., a department store with colored dresses). 4. **Reflect on the Deeper Issue** - Your discomfort with white dresses might stem from **unprocessed emotions** about your parents’ divorce. If this feels heavy, consider: - A **therapy session** (even one) to unpack it. - Talking to your fiancé about how this choice feels personal to you. --- ### **Final Thought** You **weren’t cruel**, but you **failed to communicate with empathy**. The fact that you’re **already questioning whether you did wrong** shows you’re a thoughtful person—**that’s the important part**. The apology (if you feel it) should be **light, sincere, and focused on the *how*, not the *what***. **You’re allowed to have preferences that don’t align with tradition.** The goal isn’t to please your mother—it’s to **honor your own vision** while navigating her emotions with care. That’s the adult thing to do. Would you like help drafting a message to her?
